Getting Started with tidycreel

Source: vignettes/tidycreel.Rmd
tidycreel.Rmd

Introduction

tidycreel gives fisheries biologists a tidy, pipe-friendly way to design and analyse creel surveys. You work with the terms used in the field (dates, strata, counts, interviews) without handling the internals of the survey package.

This tutorial analyses one complete season, start to finish. A clerk worked a lake for 120 days, from May 1 to August 28. On 36 of those days the clerk made an instantaneous count of anglers and interviewed angling parties, both those that had finished fishing and some still fishing. The questions are the usual ones: how much fishing happened over the season, how many fish were caught, and how many were kept.

Each answer is built from the one before:

calendar -> design
counts             -> effort        (angler-hours)
interviews         -> catch rate    (fish per angler-hour)
effort x rate      -> total catch   (fish)

The season 

library(tidycreel)

data(example_season_calendar)
data(example_season_counts)
data(example_season_interviews)

head(example_season_calendar)
#>         date day_type sampled
#> 1 2024-05-01  weekday   FALSE
#> 2 2024-05-02  weekday   FALSE
#> 3 2024-05-03  weekday   FALSE
#> 4 2024-05-04  weekend   FALSE
#> 5 2024-05-05  weekend   FALSE
#> 6 2024-05-06  weekday    TRUE
table(example_season_calendar$day_type, example_season_calendar$sampled)
#>          
#>           FALSE TRUE
#>   weekday    58   28
#>   weekend    26    8

The calendar lists every day of the season, not only the sampled ones, and splits them into weekdays and weekends. The clerk sampled 28 of the 86 weekdays and 8 of the 34 weekend days. That list of every day is what lets tidycreel expand from the days that were sampled to the whole season.

Survey design 

design <- creel_design(example_season_calendar, date = date, strata = day_type)
design
#> 
#> ── Creel Survey Design ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Type: "instantaneous"
#> Date column: date
#> Strata: day_type
#> Calendar: 120 days (2024-05-01 to 2024-08-28)
#> day_type: 2 levels
#> Counts: "none"
#> Interviews: "none"
#> Sections: "none"

creel_design() uses tidy selectors, so you name columns without quotes. The design records the 120-day calendar and its two strata.

Counts 

head(example_season_counts)
#>         date day_type total_anglers daylight_hours
#> 1 2024-05-06  weekday             5             14
#> 2 2024-05-07  weekday             5             14
#> 3 2024-05-09  weekday             9             14
#> 4 2024-05-21  weekday             3             14
#> 5 2024-05-22  weekday             7             14
#> 6 2024-06-01  weekend             2             14

design <- add_counts(design, example_season_counts,
  count_col = total_anglers,
  period_length_col = daylight_hours
)

Each row is one instantaneous count: the number of anglers fishing at the moment the clerk looked. A count is a number of anglers, not an amount of effort. To turn it into effort, tidycreel needs to know how much time the count stands for. Here the single count on each day represents the whole 14-hour fishing day, so daylight_hours is the period length. Effort for a day is the count times that length, in angler-hours.

Leaving out period_length_col still gives an estimate, but its unit is unknown, and estimate_effort() warns that no period length was supplied. tidycreel derives units from what you give it and never assumes one.

Effort

There are two different questions you can ask of these counts.

estimate_effort(design)
#> 
#> ── Creel Survey Estimates ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Method: Total
#> Variance: Taylor linearization
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> Effort target: sampled_days
#> Unit: angler-hours
#> 
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   estimate    se se_between se_within ci_lower ci_upper     n
#>      <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1     3066  386.       386.         0    2282.    3850.    36
estimate_effort(design, target = "period_total")
#> 
#> ── Creel Survey Estimates ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Method: Total
#> Variance: Taylor linearization
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> Effort target: period_total
#> Unit: angler-hours
#> 
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   estimate    se se_between se_within ci_lower ci_upper     n
#>      <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1    9994. 1286.      1286.         0    7380.   12609.    36

The first estimate, the default, is the effort on the 36 days that were sampled: 3,066 angler-hours. The second is the effort over the whole 120-day season, about 9,994 angler-hours. That season total is the number usually reported. Each stratum’s mean daily effort is multiplied by the number of days in that stratum, then the strata are added. For a season total, ask for target = "period_total".

The standard error comes from the day-to-day variation among the sampled days within each stratum. With one count per day the within-day variation (when in the day each count happened to fall) cannot be estimated separately, so se_within is 0 as a placeholder, not because activity was steady through the day. It becomes non-zero when a day has several counts. With one count per day the standard error also leaves out the finite-population correction, so it is slightly conservative; vignette("effort-pipeline") explains why.

Estimates can be broken down by any column in the design with by:

estimate_effort(design, by = day_type, target = "period_total")
#> 
#> ── Creel Survey Estimates ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Method: Total
#> Variance: Taylor linearization
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> Grouped by: day_type
#> Effort target: period_total
#> Unit: angler-hours
#> 
#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#>   day_type estimate    se se_between se_within ci_lower ci_upper     n
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1 weekday     7912  1063.      1063.         0    5753.   10071.    28
#> 2 weekend     2082.  725.       725.         0     609.    3556.     8

The 86 weekdays account for most of the season’s effort, about 7,900 angler-hours to the weekends’ 2,100. Per day, the two are closer: about 92 angler-hours on an average weekday and 61 on an average weekend day.

Interviews 

head(example_season_interviews)
#>         date day_type interview_id trip_status hours_fished n_anglers
#> 1 2024-05-06  weekday            1  incomplete         1.78         2
#> 2 2024-05-06  weekday            2  incomplete         1.82         1
#> 3 2024-05-06  weekday            3    complete         4.66         3
#> 4 2024-05-06  weekday            4    complete         0.77         2
#> 5 2024-05-07  weekday            5    complete         3.12         1
#> 6 2024-05-07  weekday            6    complete         2.23         3
#>   catch_total catch_kept
#> 1           0          0
#> 2           3          1
#> 3           1          0
#> 4           0          0
#> 5           5          0
#> 6           0          0

design <- add_interviews(design, example_season_interviews,
  catch = catch_total,
  harvest = catch_kept,
  effort = hours_fished,
  trip_status = trip_status,
  n_anglers = n_anglers
)
#> ℹ 153 interviews have zero catch.
#>   Zero catch is usual; check it is not missing data recorded as 0.
#> ℹ Added 231 interviews: 172 complete (74%), 59 incomplete (26%)

Each row is one party. add_interviews() checks the interviews as it attaches them and reports what it found: 172 complete trips, 59 incomplete, and 153 parties that caught nothing. Most anglers on most fisheries go home without a fish, and those zeros belong in the catch rate. The count is shown because, on a real data sheet, a column of zeros can also mean a catch that was never recorded. If your zeros are real, as these are, there is nothing to fix.

n_anglers matters. hours_fished is how long the party fished, so it is in party-hours. A party of three fishing two hours put in six angler-hours, and n_anglers lets tidycreel make that conversion. The catch rate is then in fish per angler-hour, the same footing as the counts. Without it the rate would be per party-hour, which cannot be multiplied by effort in angler-hours.

Catch rates 

estimate_catch_rate(design)
#> ℹ Using complete trips for CPUE estimation
#>   (n=172, 74.5% of 231 interviews) [default]
#> 
#> ── Creel Survey Estimates ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Method: Ratio-of-Means CPUE
#> Variance: Taylor linearization
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> Unit: fish/angler-hour
#> 
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   estimate     se ci_lower ci_upper     n
#>      <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1    0.221 0.0415    0.139    0.302   172
estimate_harvest_rate(design)
#> ℹ Filtering to complete trips for HPUE estimation
#>   (n=172, 74.5% of 231 interviews) [default]
#> 
#> ── Creel Survey Estimates ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Method: Ratio-of-Means HPUE
#> Variance: Taylor linearization
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> Unit: fish/angler-hour
#> 
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   estimate     se ci_lower ci_upper     n
#>      <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1   0.0639 0.0135   0.0375   0.0903   172

The catch rate is about 0.22 fish per angler-hour, and the harvest rate about 0.06. Both are ratio-of-means estimates, total catch divided by total effort across the interviews. By default they use only the 172 complete trips. A party interviewed while still fishing is more likely to be met the longer it stays, so incomplete trips over-represent long trips (length-of-stay bias) and give a biased catch rate unless the rate is steady through a trip. vignette("incomplete-trips") covers when and how incomplete trips can be used.

Total catch and harvest 

estimate_total_catch(design, target = "period_total")
#> 
#> ── Creel Survey Estimates ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Method: Total Catch (Effort × CPUE)
#> Variance: Taylor linearization
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> Effort target: period_total
#> Unit: fish
#> 
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   estimate    se ci_lower ci_upper     n
#>      <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1    2230.  506.    1231.    3230.   172
estimate_total_harvest(design, target = "period_total")
#> 
#> ── Creel Survey Estimates ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Method: Total Harvest (Effort × HPUE)
#> Variance: Taylor linearization
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> Effort target: period_total
#> Unit: fish
#> 
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   estimate    se ci_lower ci_upper     n
#>      <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1     648.  159.     334.     962.   172

A total is effort times rate, with the uncertainty of both carried into its standard error. The unit follows: angler-hours times fish per angler-hour is fish. About 2,230 fish were caught over the season, and about 650 were kept. These totals take target too, and need target = "period_total" for the season, just as effort does.

Totals break down the same way as effort:

estimate_total_catch(design, by = day_type, target = "period_total")
#> 
#> ── Creel Survey Estimates ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Method: Total Catch (Effort × CPUE)
#> Variance: Taylor linearization
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> Grouped by: day_type
#> Effort target: period_total
#> Unit: fish
#> 
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   day_type estimate    se ci_lower ci_upper     n
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1 weekday     1647.  418.   820.      2475.   138
#> 2 weekend      583.  285.     3.56    1163.    34

Released fish come from species-level catch records, attached with add_catch(), rather than from the interview totals; see ?estimate_total_release.

Using results as data

An estimate prints with its method, variance method and unit. It is not itself a data frame, so dplyr verbs do not work on it directly. Convert it first. as_tibble() returns one row per estimate, with the metadata copied into columns so it stays attached to every row:

catch_by_day <- estimate_total_catch(design, by = day_type, target = "period_total")
catch_tbl <- tibble::as_tibble(catch_by_day)
catch_tbl
#> # A tibble: 2 × 12
#>   day_type estimate    se ci_lower ci_upper     n method              estimator 
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <int> <chr>               <chr>     
#> 1 weekday     1647.  418.   820.      2475.   138 product-total-catch ratio-of-…
#> 2 weekend      583.  285.     3.56    1163.    34 product-total-catch ratio-of-…
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: variance_method <chr>, conf_level <dbl>,
#> #   effort_target <chr>, unit <chr>

catch_tbl[catch_tbl$day_type == "weekend", c("day_type", "estimate", "se", "unit")]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   day_type estimate    se unit 
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <dbl> <chr>
#> 1 weekend      583.  285. fish

as.data.frame() does the same for base R. Use metadata = FALSE for the estimates table alone.

Plotting

Estimates have an autoplot() method that draws each estimate with its confidence interval:

ggplot2::autoplot(catch_by_day)

vignette("visualisation") covers the other plots.

Variance methods

Standard errors use Taylor linearization by default. Bootstrap and jackknife replicates are also available, for effort and for every estimate built on it:

set.seed(123)
estimate_effort(design, target = "period_total", variance = "bootstrap")
#> 
#> ── Creel Survey Estimates ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Method: Total
#> Variance: Bootstrap
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> Effort target: period_total
#> Unit: angler-hours
#> 
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   estimate    se se_between se_within ci_lower ci_upper     n
#>      <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1    9994. 1342.      1342.         0    7267.   12722.    36
estimate_effort(design, target = "period_total", variance = "jackknife")
#> 
#> ── Creel Survey Estimates ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Method: Total
#> Variance: Jackknife
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> Effort target: period_total
#> Unit: angler-hours
#> 
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   estimate    se se_between se_within ci_lower ci_upper     n
#>      <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1    9994. 1286.      1286.         0    7380.   12609.    36
  • Taylor linearization (default) is fast and appropriate for most estimates.
  • Bootstrap resamples sampled days. Use it to check the linearization or for statistics that are not smooth.
  • Jackknife is deterministic, so it gives the same answer on every run.

vignette("replicate-designs") compares them.

Next steps

This tutorial used the most common design: instantaneous counts and access interviews, with weekday and weekend strata. From here:

  • vignette("survey-scheduling") builds the sampling calendar before the season, including high-use periods such as openers.
  • vignette("interview-estimation") and vignette("incomplete-trips") cover catch-rate estimators in depth.
  • vignette("section-estimation") handles lakes split into sections.
  • The Survey Types articles cover bus-route, ice, camera, aerial and mark-recapture designs.
  • vignette("glossary") defines the terms used throughout.
